---
title: "Logistic Regression in R"
format: html
---

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw())
```

Has the probability of detecting a little brown bat declined since white-nose syndrome reached West Virginia in 2009? We’ll use survey data from the Monongahela National Forest (Johnson et al. 2021).

1. Visualize the data
2. Fit the model
3. Interpret the coefficients
4. Convert log odds to probabilities
5. Visualize the predictions

## Visualize the Data

Each row is one survey of one site in one year. detected is 1 if any bats of that species were counted, 0 otherwise.

```{r}
bats <- read_csv("/courses/EDS222/data/5bat_count_data-21682.csv") |>
  # Keep only little brown bats
  filter(Species == "Myotis lucifugus")
```

What proportion of sites had detections each year?

```{r}
bats_by_year <- bats |>
  summarize(p_detected = mean(detected), .by = Year)

bats_by_year
```

Visualize the response. With a binary response, jitter the points so they don’t overlap. Add the annual proportion as a line.

```{r}
ggplot(bats, aes(x = Year, y = detected)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0.2),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = p_detected),
    data = bats_by_year,
    linewidth = 2,
    color = "cornflowerblue"
  ) +
  labs(y = "Detected")
```

## Fit the Model

Our model in statistical notation is:

Detected ~ Bernoulli(p)
logit(p) = beta_0 + beta_1(Year)

Use glm() to fit a logistic regression. The formula works like lm(), but there are two differences.

1. We have to specify the distribution of the response. For binary outcomes, use the binomial family.
2. We have to say which function links the linear equation to the expected outcome. This is where you specify the logit function.

```{r}
bat_glm <- glm(detected ~ Year, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = bats)
```

## Interpret the coefficients

```{r}
summary(bat_glm)
```

Each year, the log odds of detecting a little brown bat change by -0.2835.

Let’s convert to probabilities.

## Convert log odds to probabilities

First, create a prediction grid, which is the combination of predictor variables we want to estimate for. In this case, we only have the one predictor.

```{r}
bat_pred_grid <- tibble(
  Year = seq(2003, 2019, length.out = 101)
)
```

Next, use the predict() function to the get the probability of detection estimated by the model.

```{r}
bat_pred_grid$p_detected <- predict(
  bat_glm,
  type = "response", # Tell us the prediction on the response scale
  newdata = bat_pred_grid
)
```

## Visualize the predictions

Overlay the predicted probabilities on the raw data.

```{r}
ggplot(bats, aes(x = Year, y = detected)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0.2),
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = p_detected),
    data = bat_pred_grid,
    color = "cornflowerblue",
    linewidth = 2
  ) +
  labs(y = "Detected")
```

## Recap

- Visualize binary outcome data two ways: raw data with geom_point() (jittered) and binned summaries with geom_line() (summarize first)
- Fit a logistic model using glm()
    - Set the family to binomial()
    - Set the link to "logit"
- Visualize model predictions by:
    1. Create a prediction grid, covering the range of your predictor(s)
    2. Use predict() to get the predicted probabilities
    - Set newdata to your prediction grid (or you’ll get predictions for your raw data)
    - Set type to "response" (or you’ll get the log odds)
    3. Overlay the predicted probabilities on the raw data
